article.overview: An emission spectrometer, as the Lunar Payloads Explorer catalogue uses the term, is an instrument that measures the spectrum of infrared radiation emitted by the lunar surface and uses that spectrum to infer surface temperature and composition. The catalogue entry names a class of instruments rather than one design, so this article describes the measurement approach and three documented examples: the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment [1][2], the Chandrayaan-2 Imaging Infra-Red Spectrometer (IIRS) [4][5], and the Apollo 17 Infrared Scanning Radiometer [6]. Diviner and IIRS are orbital instruments that are documented as flown or operating. The Apollo 17 instrument is an earlier broadband radiometer, included for historical context rather than as a spectrometer.
article.description: Every object above absolute zero emits thermal radiation, and the amount and wavelength distribution of that radiation depend on its temperature and on the material's emissivity. An emission spectrometer points a telescope or optical system at the surface, separates the incoming infrared radiation into wavelength bands, and records the signal in each band. The result is a spectrum that can be compared with the spectra of known minerals and with temperature models. In lunar work the term refers to this thermal or infrared emission of the surface. It is different from the atomic emission lines that a laser-induced plasma instrument analyses, and it is different from the reflected sunlight that a reflectance spectrometer measures. The catalogue lists a separate entry for a thermal emission spectrometer, and the boundary between the two entries is not defined in the catalogue. This article therefore adopts a working scope that includes instruments whose primary measurement is emitted infrared radiation, and it discloses that choice in the limitations sections.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of thermal-infrared emission measurements on the Moon is to map surface temperature and composition at a scale that visible imagery cannot reach. Diviner was designed to measure reflected solar and emitted infrared radiation in order to characterise the lunar thermal environment, map surface properties such as thermal inertia, rock abundance and silicate mineralogy, and locate volatile cold traps in the polar regions [1][2]. Its mineralogy channels are placed near 8 micrometres to locate the Christiansen feature, a wavelength of emissivity maximum that shifts with silicate composition [2]. IIRS extends coverage into the near-infrared and short-wave infrared, from 0.8 to 5.0 micrometres, with the stated objectives of global mineralogical and volatile mapping and characterisation of the hydroxyl and water feature near 3.0 micrometres [4]. The Apollo 17 infrared radiometer mapped thermal emission from orbit, and its authors noted that night-time surface temperatures are sensitive to surface thermal properties because little heat conducts into the subsurface [6].
article.operating_principle: The surface emits as a grey or selective body whose spectral radiance follows Planck's law, modified by emissivity. Because the emitted spectrum depends on both temperature and emissivity, instruments usually combine several spectral bands. Diviner uses nine channels defined by interference and mesh filters, placed on two boresighted telescopes that focus radiation onto uncooled thermopile detectors [1]. The telescopes are scanned across the surface in a pushbroom arrangement, so each orbit builds up a line of pixels [2]. IIRS is a hyperspectral imager that disperses light with an Offner-type grating spectrometer and records about 250 contiguous bands [4][5]. Across its range the measured signal combines reflected sunlight, which dominates at the shorter wavelengths, with thermal emission from the surface. The sources reviewed here do not give the split between the two contributions, so this article does not quantify it. The Apollo 17 radiometer used a scanning optical system on the command and service module to build a thermal map of the surface [6].
article.scientific_importance: Emitted thermal infrared radiation is one of the few remote-sensing measurements that links the temperature of a lunar surface to its composition. Visible imagery shows albedo and morphology well, but it does not directly show how strongly a surface cools at night or where a mineral-diagnostic emission feature lies. Diviner was designed to characterise the thermal environment across the Moon, including the locations and temperatures of polar volatile cold traps [1][2]. IIRS adds a continuous spectral view at the wavelengths where hydroxyl and water features occur [4]. The Apollo-era radiometer demonstrated that thermal mapping from orbit was feasible, while its coarse resolution limited the detail that could be resolved [6].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a lunar emission spectrometer. Instruments differ in channel count, spectral range, optics, detector technology and platform, and the examples below describe specific instruments. The values come from the sources listed in each example and should not be read as typical of the class.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: All three examples are orbital and operate in a vacuum with no atmosphere to absorb or scatter the infrared signal. Diviner's telescopes are mounted on an articulated elevation and azimuth mechanism that lets them view the surface, deep space and calibration targets [1]. Its detectors are uncooled thermopiles, so the instrument does not rely on a cryogenic cooler [1]. Thermal channels are most informative at night, when reflected sunlight does not dominate the signal, while the solar channels need illuminated terrain [2][6]. Night-time observations depend on the thermal inertia of the surface, which is itself one of the quantities being measured [6]. Environmental tolerance limits, radiation hardness and lifetime figures were not verified for any of the three examples.
article.limitations: Emission spectra mix temperature and composition, so a single spectral feature can be hard to interpret without thermal modelling. Each pixel averages the surface within its field of view. Diviner's pixel is roughly 179 by 307 metres [2], so small rock and mineral patches are blended. Orbital data also depend on local time of day, because the surface temperature changes strongly between day and night. IIRS combines reflected and emitted signals across its range, and the sources reviewed do not separate them. Several published values differ between sources, as described in the limitations sections below. None of the examples is a surface instrument, so the lunar surface constraints that apply to a landed emission spectrometer, such as dust, thermal cycling and power, are not assessed by these examples.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: All three examples were carried by orbiting spacecraft, so their transportation history is the history of the host spacecraft. Diviner flew on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter [1][3]. IIRS was carried on the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter [4]. The Apollo 17 radiometer was carried on the command and service module [6]. No surface emission spectrometer deployment is documented in the sources reviewed for this article.
transportation_process: Integration: the instrument is mounted on the host spacecraft and connected to its power, command and data systems. Diviner's articulated pointing mount is described in [1].
Launch and lunar transfer: the spacecraft launches on a launch vehicle and reaches the Moon by a transfer trajectory. The details for each example were not retrieved in this run.

Orbit insertion and commissioning: the spacecraft enters lunar orbit, and the instrument is checked out and pointed. Diviner's mount can point at calibration targets [1]; commissioning details were not retrieved.
Routine operations: the instrument observes the surface on a fixed schedule, and its data are downlinked to Earth. Data rates for Diviner are given in [2].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not applicable to the examples described here, which were orbital instruments with no surface deployment. A landed emission spectrometer would need a mechanical mount with a clear view of the surface, thermal interfaces and a data path to the lander or rover. No such deployment was verified in this article.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 17 radiometer mapped thermal emission from lunar orbit in the early 1970s [6]. Diviner has operated on LRO since the spacecraft flew on LRO, which launched in 2009 [1][3]. IIRS extended the approach to hyperspectral coverage on Chandrayaan-2 [4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander, rover or other spacecraft compatibility is asserted for any surface-based emission spectrometer. The three examples are orbital, and their host-spacecraft interfaces are documented only at the level described in the cited sources.

article.historical_significance: Thermal emission measurements of the Moon began with orbital radiometers in the Apollo era [6]. Diviner brought multi-channel thermal mapping to the Moon with a finer footprint and a broader channel set [1][2]. IIRS extended the work into hyperspectral mapping of hydroxyl and water features [4][5]. The historical record shows that thermal and spectral emission data are complementary to reflectance data, but the sources reviewed here do not quantify how much each contributes to recent lunar science.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- Catalogue scope: the entry 'Emission spectrometer' is not defined in the catalogue and overlaps in concept with the separate 'Thermal emission spectrometer' entry. This article's scope is a working interpretation.
- Diviner mass and power (11.0 kg, 24.7 W) come from a pre-launch mission summary [3]. They were not checked against Diviner's instrument documentation in this run.
- Diviner band edges differ between sources. The EPSC 2011 abstract lists thermal bands of 13 to 23, 25 to 41, 50 to 100 and 100 to 400 micrometres. A PDS catalogue description, as summarised in search results, gives the thermal channels as starting at 12.5 micrometres. The primary PDS software interface specification should be checked before the band edges are used.
- Diviner spectral coverage of 0.3 to 400 micrometres is taken from the Paige et al. abstract text in search results [1]. The full paper was not retrieved.
- IIRS spectral resolution is given as about 20 nm in one ISRO passage and as about 20 to 25 nm in another. The band count is about 250 in ISRO's text and 256 in a second Current Science paper, which was not fetched.
- IIRS mass, power and mission-level swath are not verified from a primary handbook. The 20 km swath comes from a Current Science table summarised in search results [5].
- The IIRS image identity rests on ISRO's caption 'Imaging Infra-Red Spectrometer (IIRS)'. The same caption also appears on a TMC-2 image on the same page, so the caption itself is not independently confirmed.
- The Apollo 17 radiometer details come from a search-result summary of a 1974 paper [6]. Mass, power and channel details were not verified.
- Operational status of Diviner and IIRS as of 2026 was not verified in this run. The article describes them as flown or operating only where a source says so.
- No surface emission spectrometer is documented here, so the article makes no surface-operations or landing-site claims.
